title: Streaming webhook retry strategies and deduplication guide
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Overview

This guide describes recommended patterns for delivering high-throughput streaming events from Redwood APIs (or any Redwood-backed pipeline) to customer webhook endpoints with robust retry behavior and deduplication. It is intended for technical owners on both Redwood and customer sides: customer-success engineers, integration engineers, SREs, and platform teams.

Goals

- Maximize end-to-end delivery success while maintaining predictable latency and avoiding duplicate side effects at customer systems.
- Provide concrete recommended retry schedules, idempotency semantics, and storage/TTL guidance for deduplication keys.
- Define observability, runbook steps, and escalation ownership for webhook delivery incidents.

Delivery semantics primer

- At-least-once: Redwood attempts delivery until success or an expiry condition; duplicates are possible and customers must guard against repeated processing.
- Best-effort exactly-once: Achieved by combining idempotency keys + deduplication windows at the recipient. The architecture below describes how to approach this pattern.

SLOs and thresholds (examples)

- Successful first-attempt delivery rate: >= 99.0% over 30d for customer endpoints with 200ms median response times.
- End-to-end success within retry window: >= 99.9% over 30d.
- Mean time to detect webhook delivery outage (alerting): <= 5 minutes.
- Duplicate delivery rate (observed duplicates processed): <= 0.05% for well-instrumented customers.

When to apply these patterns

- Recommended for event-driven integrations with side effects (billing, user notification, state mutation).
- Optional for purely idempotent / read-only consumers (batch analytics webhooks may accept relaxed deduplication).

Recommended architecture (high level)

1) Redwood outbound delivery service (owned by eng-infra/eng-platform): persistent queue, per-customer delivery workers, per-destination backoff and concurrency limits.
2) Delivery metadata: include a stable event_id, event_type, timestamp, and an idempotency_key header.
3) Recipient deduplication store: short-lived datastore (Redis, DynamoDB with TTL attributes, or Postgres table with TTL enforcement) keyed by idempotency_key/event_id.

Message contract (required fields)

- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Event-ID: <uuid-v4>
- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Event-Type: <string>
- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key: <sha256 or custom>
- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=HEX_SIGNATURE (see Security section)
- Body: JSON payload with an explicit "event_version" and canonical "payload" object.

Example payload

{
  "event_version": "1.0",
  "payload": {
    "user_id": "acct_123",
    "action": "model.inference.completed",
    "meta": {"model": "redwood-llm-v2", "latency_ms": 142}
  }
}

HTTP status mapping and recommendations

- 200 / 2xx: Success — Redwood marks delivery succeeded and stops retries.
- 429: Throttle — treat as transient. Retry using exponential backoff with jitter.
- 5xx: Transient server error — retry using exponential backoff with capped max interval.
- 408 / 499 / network errors: Transient — retry.
- 4xx (400, 401, 403): Permanent failure (client code issue or auth). Do not retry automatically; surface to integrations team and customer.

Recommended retry schedule (example)

- Immediate retry policy with exponential backoff + jitter. Conservative schedule used across Redwood: 

  Attempt 1: 0s (initial)
  Attempt 2: 5s + jitter (0-2s)
  Attempt 3: 30s + jitter (0-10s)
  Attempt 4: 2m + jitter (0-30s)
  Attempt 5: 10m + jitter (0-60s)
  Attempt 6: 1h + jitter (0-10m) — final attempt before expiry

- Default expiry window: 6 hours for non-critical events; 24–72 hours for business-critical events (negotiated in contract).
- Note: Customers may configure shorter windows in their destination configuration.

Idempotency and deduplication guidance

1) Idempotency key content: preferred: stable event_id (UUID v4) or sha256(event_id || tenant_id).
2) Deduplication window: set TTL = min(expiry_window + 10%, 7d). For typical 6h expiry, TTL ~7h. For 72h expiry, TTL ~4d.
3) Storage options:
   - Redis: fast checks, set NX with TTL. Good for sub-day windows.
   - DynamoDB: durable, can store more metadata; use TTL attribute and conditional put.
   - Postgres: use unique constraint on (event_id, tenant_id) with background cleanup; better if you already have transactional DB.
4) Accept-late-arrival semantic: if a duplicate arrives outside TTL, treat as new event or log as late duplicate per customer policy.

Example dedup pseudocode (Redis)

// pseudo-code
IF SETNX("dedupe:<idempotency_key>", "1", EXPIRE=ttl_seconds) == 1:
  // first-seen -> process
ELSE:
  // duplicate -> ack (200) and skip processing

Security: signature verification and replay protection

- Redwood signs payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using per-customer webhook secret. Signature is included in X-Redwood-Signature. Example header: 
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=4b6f...

- Verification example (pseudo-shell):
  expected=$(echo -n "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$WEBHOOK_SECRET")
  if [ "$expected" != "$HEADER_SIG" ]; then reject (401)

- Replay protection: ensure idempotency_key and dedupe store are used. Optionally enforce timestamp freshness (X-Redwood-Timestamp) rejecting events older than a configurable window (default 24h).

Observability and metrics (instrumentation)

- Metrics to emit: delivery_attempts_total, delivery_success_total, delivery_failures_by_status_code, delivery_latency_ms_histogram, duplicate_events_acked_total, per_destination_concurrency, per_destination_queue_depth.
- Dashboards: per-customer delivery success rate, rolling-24h failure rate, average retry count, and top 10 failing endpoints.
- Alerts: trigger when a single destination has >1% failure rate over 10m and >100 attempts, or when delivery latency p50 > 5s for 5m.

Testing and validation checklist (for customers)

1) Provide a stable webhook endpoint that responds to GET or 200 to validate.
2) Share webhook secret for signature verification testing (use staging secret first).
3) Validate idempotency behavior by sending the same X-Redwood-Event-ID twice: first should be processed, second should be acknowledged without duplicate side effect.
4) Load test: exercise 10–50 rps for a sandbox destination to validate rate limiting and concurrency.

Sample curl test (signature omitted for brevity)

curl -X POST https://myendpoint.example.com/webhooks \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Event-ID: 9f8e7c1e-...-4a12' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key: 9f8e7c1e-...-4a12' \
  -d '{"event_version":"1.0","payload":{"action":"model.inference.completed","user_id":"acct_123"}}'

Operational runbook (common failure scenarios)

- Scenario: Large spike of 5xx errors from customer endpoint.
  1) Automatically increase backoff and reduce per-destination concurrency to 1 for 30m.
  2) Post incident in #cs-integrations with destination id, sample failures, and last successful timestamp.
  3) Notify customer success owner and schedule call if >30% messages failing after 1h.

- Scenario: Customer responding 4xx to all requests (401/403).
  1) Mark destination as "authentication error" in admin UI and suspend retries.
  2) Open a ticket to customer contacts, include sample request/response, and request resolution.

- Scenario: Duplicate processing observed by customer.
  1) Verify event IDs from logs and delivery requests.
  2) Confirm dedupe store TTL and existence.
  3) If Redwood caused duplicate replays (bug), escalate to eng-serving-runtime and run a hotfix rollout.

Rollout checklist for new customer webhook integration

- Pre-onboarding: confirm recipient supports HTTPS: TLS 1.2+, can verify HMAC signatures, provides a single stable URL, and has an owner + escalation contact.
- Sandbox phase (0–2 days): set up staging secret, run smoke tests, observe 100% first-attempt success in sandbox.
- Pilot phase (2–7 days): ramp to partial traffic (5–20%); monitor error rate and latency; exercise retries and dup detection.
- Go-live: switch route config to 100% traffic and maintain elevated monitoring for 72h.

Ownership and escalation

- Day-to-day owner: customer-success integrations engineer (CS Integrations).
- Escalation path: CS Integrations -> SRE oncall -> Eng Platform -> Eng Serving Runtime.
- Communication templates: include: event_id list, sample timestamps, last 10 delivery responses, and suggested action items.

Compatibility notes with Redwood features

- Batching and KV cache: if the webhook is triggered by a batched job (e.g., model inference group), events should include a batch_id in the payload to allow customers to coalesce processing.
- Model variant fallbacks: if Redwood automatically routes to a fallback model, event metadata will include fallback.reason and fallback.replaced_model. Customers should treat these events identically unless they filter by model.

Appendix A — Example headers and signature verification (Node.js snippet)

const crypto = require('crypto')
function verifySignature(body, headerSig, secret) {
  const expected = 'sha256=' + crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(body).digest('hex')
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(headerSig))
}

Appendix B — Example DynamoDB dedupe item (JSON)

{
  "EventId": "9f8e7c1e-...",
  "TenantId": "acct_123",
  "CreatedAt": "2026-01-20T15:12:34Z",
  "TTL": 1700000000
}
